passages.happening:
The LORD tells Noah, “Go into the ark, you and all your family, because I have found you righteous in this generation” (verse 1).

Noah is to take seven pairs of every kind of clean animal, one pair of every kind of unclean animal, and seven pairs of every kind of bird, “to preserve their offspring on the face of all the earth” (verses 2-3). In seven days God will send rain for forty days and forty nights (verse 4). “And Noah did all that the LORD had commanded him” (verse 5).

Noah is 600 years old (verse 6). He goes in with his wife, his sons and their wives (verse 7). The animals come “two by two, male and female, as God had commanded Noah” (verse 9). After seven days the floodwaters come (verse 10).
passages.hearers:
Israel's later law sorted animals into ‘clean’ and ‘unclean’. Clean animals could be eaten and offered to God; unclean ones could not (Leviticus 11). Genesis assumes Noah already knows the difference. The extra clean animals will be needed: for Noah's offering after the flood (8:20), and for food, since God will allow people to eat meat (9:3).

The Hebrew for ‘seven pairs’ is literally ‘seven seven’. It can mean seven pairs or seven animals in all, and Bibles translate it both ways.

Notice the waiting. God gives seven days' warning. The door is open a little longer. And notice the repeated line: Noah did all that God commanded. The story slows down to let the reader see it. Noah's faith is shown not in words, but in doing what he was told.
passages.later:
Jesus describes this week before the flood: “People were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, up to the day Noah entered the ark. Then the flood came and destroyed them all” (Luke 17:27). They were not doing anything strange. They simply did not believe it was coming.

Peter says God “waited patiently in the days of Noah while the ark was being built” (1 Peter 3:20). The seven days are part of that patience.

Hebrews says Noah obeyed “when warned about things not yet seen” (Hebrews 11:7). Faith in the Bible often looks like this: acting on God's word before you can see why.
passages.hard:
In chapter 6 God says to bring two of every kind (6:19-20). Here he says seven pairs of the clean animals and of the birds (7:2-3). How do these fit?

Many readers take chapter 6 as the general rule, two of every kind to keep each kind alive, and chapter 7 as the added detail, more of the clean animals for sacrifice and food. On this reading the second command fills out the first.

Many scholars think the flood story was woven together from two older accounts, each with its own numbers and its own name for God (‘God’ in 6:22 and ‘the LORD’ in 7:5). On this reading the writer kept both, side by side.

These notes do not choose. Either way the story as we have it makes sense: every kind is kept alive, and clean animals are kept for worship.
passages.asks: God gave seven days of warning, and the door stayed open. Ask whether there is something God has been warning you about, and whether you are using the time he gives. And ask what it would look like to obey before you can see the reason.

passages.t: The deep breaks open, and God shuts the door
passages.happening:
The text gives a date: “In the six hundredth year of Noah’s life, on the seventeenth day of the second month” (verse 11). On that day “all the fountains of the great deep burst forth, and the floodgates of the heavens were opened.” Rain falls for forty days and forty nights (verse 12).

Noah, his wife, his three sons and their wives go into the ark, with every kind of creature (verses 13-15). They go in “as God had commanded Noah. Then the LORD shut him in” (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
Ancient peoples pictured the world as a space held open in the middle of water. There were waters above, held back by the sky, and waters below, ‘the great deep’, which fed springs and seas. On the second and third days of creation God separated the waters and made dry land appear (1:6-10).

Now both are let loose. The fountains of the deep burst up from below. The ‘floodgates’ (literally ‘windows’) of the heavens open from above. The word for ‘the deep’, tehom, is the word of 1:2, where darkness was over the deep before God began to shape the world. The flood is creation running backward. The order God set in place is being undone.

The date is unusual. Nothing earlier in Genesis has a day and a month. From here the story reads almost like a ship's log, counting days and months.

Then one small sentence: ‘the LORD shut him in’. Noah built the ark, but God closes the door. It is God's own hand that keeps Noah safe. It also means the time for going in is over.
passages.later:
The psalms speak of God's rule over the waters: “The LORD sits enthroned over the flood; the LORD is enthroned as King forever” (Psalm 29:10). Even when the deep breaks open, it is not out of his hand.

Jesus shows the same rule when he rebukes the wind and the sea and “it was perfectly calm” (Mark 4:39).

Jesus also speaks of himself as a door: “I am the gate. If anyone enters through Me, he will be saved” (John 10:9). Many readers have heard an echo of the ark's one door, though the New Testament does not draw that link itself.
passages.hard:
The door closes, and outside are people and animals who will die. This is the hardest part of the story, and it should not be made small.

The Bible does not tell it with glee. God grieved before he judged (6:6). He waited, and gave warning. And the story's own reason is the violence that had filled the earth (6:11). Still, the text says plainly that many died, and a reader may rightly feel the weight of that. Christians believe God is the just judge of all the earth, and they also believe he takes no pleasure in anyone's death (Ezekiel 33:11). Both are in the Bible, and both are here.

If this story frightens you, remember how it ends: God promises never to do it again (9:11). If you have lived through a flood or a storm, it was not a sign that God had shut a door on you. Talk to someone you trust about what you carry, and the Find Help page has people you can call.
passages.asks: ‘The LORD shut him in.’ Noah's safety did not depend on how well he held the door. Ask where you are trying to keep yourself safe by your own strength, and what it would mean to trust the hand that closes the door.

passages.happening:
For forty days the flood comes. The waters rise and lift the ark high above the earth (verse 17). They surge and rise greatly, and the ark floats on the surface (verse 18). “Finally, the waters completely inundated the earth, so that all the high mountains under all the heavens were covered” (verse 19). The water rises fifteen cubits above the mountains (verse 20).

Then the text says plainly what happened to life on the land. Every living thing that moved on the earth perished. “Of all that was on dry land, everything that had the breath of life in its nostrils died” (verse 22). “Only Noah and those with him in the ark remained” (verse 23). The waters prevail on the earth for 150 days (verse 24).
passages.hearers:
The writing itself rises like the water. The same words come back again and again: the waters rose, then rose greatly, then covered the mountains. A listener would feel it building.

The list of creatures that died runs in the reverse of the order in which they were made in chapter 1: people, livestock, crawling creatures, birds (verse 23). The world is being unmade.

‘The breath of life’ recalls the breath God breathed into the first man (2:7). What God gave is now taken back.

The first hearers would know floods from experience. In Mesopotamia, the flat land between the Tigris and the Euphrates, river floods were a real and terrible danger. Archaeologists have found thick flood layers at ancient cities there, such as Ur, Kish and Shuruppak. In 1929 Leonard Woolley announced that the layer he found at Ur was the flood of the Bible. Later work showed that these layers come from different times and different local floods, and Woolley himself later gave up the claim. No single layer can be tied to Noah's flood.

And at the center of it all, a quiet sentence: ‘only Noah and those with him in the ark remained’. Out of a world unmade, God keeps a remnant.
passages.later:
Peter says that “the world of that time perished in the flood” (2 Peter 3:6), and sets it beside the final judgment. Jesus too uses the flood as a picture of a judgment people do not expect (Luke 17:26-27).

But the Bible also turns the flood into a promise. God tells Israel through Isaiah, “I swore that the waters of Noah would never again cover the earth. So I have sworn that I will not be angry with you or rebuke you” (Isaiah 54:9).

And it speaks to everyone who feels the waters rising. “When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and when you go through the rivers, they will not overwhelm you” (Isaiah 43:2).
passages.hard:
Did the flood cover the whole globe, or a region? Christians have read it in more than one way.

The global reading takes verse 19, ‘all the high mountains under all the heavens’, at its plain face value: the whole planet was covered. Many who hold it also think the flood explains much of the earth's rock layers, a view made widely known by John Whitcomb and Henry Morris in The Genesis Flood (1961).

The regional reading notes that the Hebrew word for ‘earth’, erets, is also the ordinary word for ‘land’, as in ‘the land of Canaan’. It notes that Genesis uses whole-world words in a limited way elsewhere: when “every nation came to Joseph in Egypt to buy grain,” the famine was “over all the earth” (41:57). On this reading the flood covered the whole world that Noah knew, and destroyed the people of that land.

Others think the writer does describe the whole earth, but tells a real memory of a great flood in the way ancient writers told such things, to teach who God is and what sin does.

Christians differ, and these notes do not settle it. On every reading the chapter teaches the same thing: God judges evil, he does not forget his own, and he keeps life alive through judgment.
passages.asks: In a chapter of rising water, the ark floats. Ask what feels like rising water in your life right now. Then read Isaiah's promise slowly: the waters will not overwhelm you. Ask whether you can trust the God who kept the ark afloat with what is pressing on you.
